mainTopic: Conflicting witnesses about קידושין and גירושין, and when a woman permitted on her own word can lose that permission, including the story of שמואל's captive daughters
overview: The amud opens by asking why a ברייתא treats conflicting witnesses about קידושין differently from conflicting witnesses about גירושין. אביי says the case is one witness against one, so the status both witnesses agree on wins. רב אשי says it is two against two, with the rulings switched. Witnesses who only say 'we didn't see' prove nothing, because people may do both קידושין and גירושין in private. Next the גמרא asks which clause of the משנה the rule 'if witnesses came after she married, she does not leave' belongs to. רבי אושעיא and רבה בר אבין disagree, and the גמרא explains their dispute through רב המנונא's rule that a woman will not lie to her husband's face. אבוה דשמואל adds that once the court permits her to marry, later witnesses cannot take that permission away, and a ברייתא about a captive woman fits this. The amud ends with the story of שמואל's daughters, who were captured, declared themselves pure before רבי חנינא and were permitted. רב אשי explains that only witnesses who saw actual violation could undo such a permission.

steps.title: Why do the first and second cases of the ברייתא differ?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא lets a woman stay married in the disputed קידושין case but forces her to leave in the disputed גירושין case.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between the first case and the second case?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the two halves of the ברייתא look alike but end differently, and it asks why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases two witnesses say one thing and two say the opposite, so the evidence seems equally balanced. Yet in the קידושין case (רישא) a woman who married may stay, while in the גירושין case (סיפא) she must leave. The גמרא wants a reason for this difference.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference? (a question that points out an inconsistency)
The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching

phrases.english: What is different in the first clause,
and what is different in the latter clause?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא, וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא quoted on the previous amud.
steps.kashyaTarget: The different rulings in the ברייתא for disputed קידושין and disputed גירושין.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two cases have the same structure, two witnesses against two, so they should end the same way.

steps.title: אביי: the case is one witness against one, and both agree she was single
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the ברייתא is about a single witness on each side. In the קידושין case, both witnesses agree she was once a פנויה, so the witness claiming קידושין stands alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Read the ברייתא as a case of one witness on each side. One witness says she received קידושין and one says she did not. Both of them are testifying that she was single. The one who says she received קידושין is just one person, and one person's word does not count against two.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question by saying the ברייתא is about one witness against one witness. He starts with the first case, about קידושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness who says 'she received קידושין' also agrees that she was single before that. So on the point that she was a פנויה, both witnesses agree, and that counts as two voices. The claim that she changed status rests on one witness alone. That is why, if she already married, she does not have to leave.

keyTerms.term: אֵין דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹם שְׁנַיִם
keyTerms.meaning: One person's word does not count against two

phrases.english: Abaye said: Interpret it as a case of one witness:
one witness says, "She was betrothed,"
and one witness says, "She was not betrothed" —
both of them are testifying about an unmarried woman,
phrases.notes: Even the witness who says she got קידושין agrees she was single before that.

phrases.english: and this one who says "She was betrothed" —
he is only one,
and the words of one have no weight
against two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1 by redefining the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case (one witness on each side rather than two)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא is about two witnesses against two, so both cases should end the same way.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is one witness against one. Both witnesses agree on her original status, so the witness claiming a change is outweighed.

steps.title: אביי continued: in the גירושין case, both agree she was married
steps.stepSummary: אביי applies the same reasoning to the גירושין case. Both witnesses agree she was once an אשת איש, so the witness claiming גירושין stands alone and she must leave.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the last case, one witness says she was divorced and one says she was not. Both of them are testifying that she was a married woman. The one who says she was divorced is just one person, and one person's word does not count against two.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his answer by applying the same logic to the second case, about גירושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the starting point both witnesses agree on is that she was an אשת איש. Only one witness says she changed status by receiving a גט. That lone claim does not override two, so she is still treated as married and must leave a second husband. The same rule leads to opposite results because the starting status is opposite.
steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, the ruling follows the status that both witnesses agree on: single in the קידושין case, married in the גירושין case. The lone witness who claims a change loses.

phrases.english: The latter clause: one witness says, "She was divorced,"
and one witness says, "She was not divorced" —
both of them are testifying about a married woman,
and this one who says "She was divorced" —
he is only one,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין דְּבָרָיו שֶׁל אֶחָד בִּמְקוֹם שְׁנַיִם.
phrases.english: and the words of one have no weight against two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's answer by applying it to the סיפא.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the גירושין case the agreed status is אשת איש, so the lone witness for a divorce is outweighed and she must leave.

steps.title: רב אשי: two against two, but switch the rulings
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי keeps the case as two witnesses against two but switches the rulings. In the קידושין case, she may not marry, and if she married she must leave.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Really it is two witnesses against two, but switch the rulings. If two say 'we saw that she received קידושין' and two say 'we did not see that she received קידושין,' she may not marry, and if she married she must leave.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a different answer. He does not change who the witnesses are. Instead, he reverses the rulings of the ברייתא, starting with the קידושין case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike אביי, רב אשי accepts that each side has two witnesses (תרי ותרי). He fixes the problem by switching the outcomes, so now the קידושין case is the strict one. Notice the new wording: the second pair says only 'we did not see' the קידושין, which is different from saying 'it did not happen.'

keyTerms.meaning: Really / actually (keeping the original case as it was)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two answers. אביי changes the witnesses to one against one and leaves the rulings alone. רב אשי keeps two against two and switches the rulings.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
Actually it is two against two, and reverse the rulings:
phrases.notes: Keep it as two witnesses on each side, but swap which half is strict and which is lenient.

phrases.english: two say, "We saw her that she was betrothed,"
and two say, "We did not see her that she was betrothed" —
this woman may not marry,
and if she married — she must leave.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: לְעוֹלָם תְּרֵי וּתְרֵי, וְאֵיפוֹךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to step 1 that differs from אביי's.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reverses the rulings of the ברייתא while keeping the case as two against two
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's rulings stand as written and only the witness setup needs to change (אביי's approach).
steps.terutzMaskana: In the קידושין case with two against two, she may not marry, and if she married she must leave.

steps.title: Isn't it obvious that 'we did not see' proves nothing?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב אשי's reading of the קידושין case. Two witnesses saying ״we didn't see her betrothed״ obviously cannot outweigh two who say they did see it.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's obvious! Saying 'we did not see her' is no proof at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא bothers to teach the קידושין ruling under רב אשי's reading. The answer seems too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רב אשי, two witnesses say they saw the קידושין, and two others only say they did not see it. Not seeing something does not mean it didn't happen. So of course she must leave, and the גמרא asks what new thing the ברייתא is teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (a challenge that a teaching adds nothing new)
We did not see her (do this)

phrases.english: It is obvious!
"We did not see her" is not proof!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's reading from Step 4 by asking what the ברייתא adds.
steps.kashyaTarget: The קידושין clause of the ברייתא as רב אשי reads it.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Testimony of not seeing cannot cancel testimony of seeing, so the ruling seems too obvious to need teaching.

steps.title: Neighbors in one courtyard, and private betrothals
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the witnesses live in the same courtyard as the woman. The ברייתא teaches that people often do קידושין privately, so even close neighbors might not know.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it's needed for a case where they live in the same courtyard. You might have said: if she really had been betrothed, word would have gotten out. So it teaches us that people do betroth in private.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the ruling is not obvious. It is about witnesses who live right next to the woman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the neighbors never heard about a קידושין, we might think it never happened, because such news usually spreads. The ברייתא teaches that people sometimes do קידושין quietly. So even neighbors who didn't see it cannot weaken the testimony of those who did.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (a special case)
The matter would become publicly known

phrases.english: No, it is necessary where they live in one courtyard.
phrases.notes: "They" means the woman and the witnesses who say they didn't see it.

phrases.english: You might have said:
If it were true that she was betrothed,
the matter would have publicity.
phrases.notes: Literally, "the matter has a voice." News like this usually spreads.

phrases.english: It teaches us
that people do betroth in private.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the פשיטא challenge of Step 5 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (לא צריכא) to a situation where the ruling is not obvious.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Neighbors who heard nothing show that no קידושין took place, because such news spreads.
steps.terutzMaskana: People do קידושין privately, so the neighbors' silence proves nothing.

steps.title: What does the divorce clause add?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the second half of the ברייתא, about two who saw the divorce against two who didn't. It asks what new idea this clause teaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: The second half: two say 'we saw her get divorced' and two say 'we did not see her get divorced.' She may not remarry, but if she did, she does not leave. What is this teaching us?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the גירושין half of the ברייתא, as רב אשי reads it. It asks the same kind of question: what is new here?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here too, the second pair only say they didn't see the divorce, which proves nothing. So the ruling that she need not leave a second marriage seems obvious. The גמרא wants to know what this clause adds.

keyTerms.meaning: The latter clause (second half) of a teaching
She may not marry (at the outset)
She does not have to leave (her husband)

phrases.english: The latter clause: two say, "We saw her that she was divorced,"
and two say, "We did not see her that she was divorced" —
this woman may not marry,
and if she married, she does not leave.
What is it teaching us?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same 'what is new here' question from Step 5 to the second half of the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What new idea the גירושין clause adds.

steps.title: Even when they live in one courtyard
steps.stepSummary: The first answer: the clause teaches that 'we didn't see' proves nothing even when the witnesses are neighbors in the same courtyard.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even though they live in the same courtyard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a quick answer that copies the earlier one. The case is about neighbors in one courtyard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer reuses the same narrowing from Step 6. Close neighbors who heard nothing about the divorce still don't weaken the witnesses who saw it.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל גַּב דְּדָיְירִי בְּחָצֵר אֶחָד —
phrases.english: Even though they live in one courtyard —

steps.triggerLanguage: אַף עַל גַּב דְּדָיְירִי בְּחָצֵר אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 by using the same courtyard setting as Step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The clause teaches that not seeing proves nothing, even when the witnesses are neighbors.

steps.title: But that is the same lesson again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that this answer just repeats the lesson already learned from the קידושין clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: That's the same thing as before!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer it just gave. The divorce clause would then teach nothing beyond what the first clause already taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause already showed that neighbors in one courtyard may not know what happens. If the second clause teaches only that, it is repeating itself. A ברייתא is not expected to say the same thing twice.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the same as that (a challenge that two teachings repeat each other)

phrases.english: This is the same as that!
phrases.notes: "That" is the courtyard lesson already taught about קידושין back in Step 6.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of Step 8 as a repeat of Step 6.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The lesson is already taught in the קידושין clause, so repeating it in the גירושין clause would be pointless.

steps.title: Divorce can also be done privately
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the new point. We might have thought only קידושין is done quietly, while a divorce always becomes public. The ברייתא teaches that people do both privately.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: it's only with betrothal that people do it in private. But with divorce, if she really was divorced, word would get out. So it teaches us that people betroth and divorce in private.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the divorce clause does teach something new. It is not a repeat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A divorce might seem like something that can't stay quiet, so neighbors' silence would mean it didn't happen. The ברייתא teaches that גירושין, like קידושין, can happen privately. That is why ״we didn't see″ still proves nothing in the divorce case.
steps.whatToRemember: Both halves of the ברייתא teach something real. Witnesses who say ״we didn't see״ prove nothing, even if they are close neighbors, because people do both קידושין and גירושין in private.

phrases.english: You might have said:
it is regarding betrothal
that people do betroth in private,
but regarding divorce,
if it were true that she was divorced,
the matter would have publicity.
It teaches us
that people do betroth and divorce in private.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: גַּבֵּי קִדּוּשִׁין הוּא דַּעֲבִידִי אִינָשֵׁי דִּמְקַדְּשִׁי בְּצִנְעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the הַיְינוּ הָךְ challenge of Step 9 by showing a separate lesson about divorce.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Showing that the second clause teaches a separate point (divorce, not just betrothal).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only קידושין is done privately. A divorce would surely become public, so neighbors' silence would show there was none.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both קידושין and גירושין can be done privately.

steps.title: Which clause of the משנה does 'she does not leave' refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's rule that if witnesses come after she married, she does not leave. רבי אושעיא applies it to the first clause, and רבה בר אבין applies it to the latter clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And if witnesses came after she married, she does not leave.' רבי אושעיא taught this on the first clause; רבה בר אבין taught it on the latter clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה and brings two אמוראים who disagree about which case that line belongs to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה has two cases where a woman is believed about herself. In the first, she says she was married and divorced. In the second, she says she was taken captive and stayed pure. The rule that she need not leave her new husband if witnesses come later is placed by רבי אושעיא on the first clause and by רבה בר אבין on the latter clause.

keyTerms.meaning: He teaches it (places this rule on a certain clause)
The first clause of a teaching
An אמורא who places the rule on the first clause
An אמורא who places the rule on the latter clause

steps.whyThisMatters: Where the rule is placed decides which woman gets the lenient ruling of not having to leave her husband.

phrases.english: "And if witnesses came after she married,
she does not leave," etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes our משנה, not the ברייתא we were just discussing.

phrases.english: Rabbi Oshaya teaches it on the first clause;
phrases.notes: The first clause is the woman who says she was married and divorced.

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר אָבִין מַתְנֵי לַהּ אַסֵּיפָא.
phrases.english: Rabba bar Avin teaches it on the latter clause.
phrases.notes: The latter clause is the woman who says she was taken captive and stayed pure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ברייתא discussion and returns to the משנה with a new question.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a disagreement over which clause the rule ״if witnesses came after she married, she does not leave״ refers to: רבי אושעיא says the first clause (divorce), רבה בר אבין says the latter clause (captivity).

steps.title: How the two views relate to each other
steps.stepSummary: Whoever applies the rule to the first clause would surely apply it to the captive woman. Whoever applies it to the captive woman would not necessarily apply it to the first clause.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who applies the rule to the first clause applies it even more to the latter clause, because the Sages were lenient with a captive woman. But the one who applies it to the latter clause would not apply it to the first clause.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the two views from the last step fit together. One view includes the other, but not the other way around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אושעיא applied 'she does not leave' to the first clause, the woman who says she was divorced. He would surely also apply it to the captive woman, because the Sages were more lenient about captives. רבה בר אבין applied it only to the captive woman, so in his view the divorced woman's case stays strict.

keyTerms.meaning: The first clause of the משנה
The latter clause of the משנה
A woman who was taken captive

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on the first clause —
phrases.notes: 'It' is the rule from the משנה that if witnesses come after she married, she does not leave.

phrases.english: all the more so on the latter clause,
since with a captive woman they were lenient.
And the one who teaches it on the latter clause,
but on the first clause — no.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּמַתְנֵי לַהּ אַרֵישָׁא כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַסֵּיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the two views quoted in step 11 relate to each other.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first-clause view includes the captive case through a קל וחומר. The latter-clause view does not include the first clause.

steps.title: Suggestion that the dispute depends on רב המנונא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא proposes that the two views argue about whether to accept רב המנונא's rule that a woman is not brazen in front of her husband.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say they argue about רב המנונא's rule? The one who applies it to the first clause holds of רב המנונא. The one who applies it to the latter clause does not hold of רב המנונא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to find the reason behind the two views. It suggests they depend on an earlier rule of רב המנונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב המנונא said a woman who tells her husband 'you divorced me' is believed, because she would not be so bold as to lie to his face. The suggestion is that the first-clause view trusts the woman's divorce claim because of this idea. The other view rejects רב המנונא, so it does not trust her.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say, a suggestion the גמרא may later reject
He does not hold of, he rejects

phrases.english: Shall we say they disagree about the rule of רב המנונא?
phrases.notes: On the previous amud, רב המנונא said a woman who tells her husband 'you divorced me' is believed, since she wouldn't dare lie to his face.

phrases.english: For the one who teaches it on the first clause
holds of רב המנונא's rule.
And the one who teaches it on the latter clause
does not hold of רב המנונא's rule.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Looks for the reason behind the two views described in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the underlying reason for the disagreement between רבי אושעיא and רבה בר אבין?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Suggested: whether they accept רב המנונא's rule.

steps.title: Both accept רב המנונא; they argue about when he is not present
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone accepts רב המנונא, but they argue whether his rule also works when the husband is not in front of her.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone holds of רב המנונא, and here they argue about this: one master holds that רב המנונא's rule was said only when she speaks in front of him, but when he is not there she is bold enough to lie. The other master holds that even when he is not there she is not bold enough.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the suggestion from step 13. It gives a different reason for the dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree a woman will not lie to her husband's face. In our משנה, the first husband who supposedly divorced her is not standing there. So they argue whether she would dare lie when he is absent. If she would, we do not trust her. If she would not, we trust her and she does not leave.

keyTerms.meaning: She is bold, she would dare to lie

steps.confusionAlert: The two views do not argue about whether רב המנונא is right. They both accept him, and only argue how far his rule reaches.

phrases.aramaic: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא.
phrases.english: No, everyone holds of רב המנונא's rule.
And here they disagree about this:

phrases.aramaic: דְּמָר סָבַר: כִּי אִיתְּמַר דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא בְּפָנָיו,
phrases.english: One master holds: when רב המנונא's rule was said, it was for in his presence,
but not in his presence — she is bold.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר סָבַר: שֶׁלֹּא בְּפָנָיו נָמֵי אֵינָהּ מְעִיזָּה.
phrases.english: And the other master holds: not in his presence too, she is not bold.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא אִית לְהוּ דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proposal of step 13 and replaces it with a narrower point of dispute.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that one side rejects רב המנונא entirely.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dispute can be explained even if both accept רב המנונא: they argue only whether his rule applies when the husband is absent.
steps.whatToRemember: Both views accept רב המנונא. They argue only whether a woman would dare lie when the husband is not in front of her.

steps.title: אבוה דשמואל: 'married' means permitted to marry
steps.stepSummary: Returning to the משנה, אבוה דשמואל says 'after she married' does not need an actual marriage. Once the court allowed her to marry, she does not leave, even if she has not married yet.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'And if witnesses came after she married.' The father of שמואל said: 'Married' does not mean really married. Rather, once they permitted her to marry, even though she has not married, the rule applies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a phrase in the משנה and gives אבוה דשמואל's explanation of the word 'married.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain reading is that the rule protects her only once she has actually remarried. אבוה דשמואל says the key moment is earlier: as soon as the court permits her to marry. After that, witnesses who come later do not take that permission away.

phrases.english: And if witnesses came after she married, etc.
The father of שמואל said:
'Married' does not mean actually married,
rather, once they permitted her to marry —
even though she has not married.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the same phrase of the משנה discussed in step 11 and explains its wording.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once the court permits her to marry, later witnesses do not undo that, even before an actual marriage.

steps.title: But the משנה says 'she does not leave'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אבוה דשמואל: the words 'she does not leave' suggest she already has a husband to leave.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it teaches 'she does not leave'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אבוה דשמואל's reading using the משנה's own words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Leave' sounds like leaving a husband. That only makes sense if she is already married. So the משנה seems to be talking about a real marriage, against אבוה דשמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: She does not leave, she does not go out

phrases.english: But it teaches 'she does not leave'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges אבוה דשמואל's reading from step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: אבוה דשמואל's claim that 'married' means only 'permitted to marry.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Not leave' implies leaving a husband, which needs an actual marriage.

steps.title: She does not lose her first permission
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'she does not leave' means she does not lose the permission to marry that she already received.
steps.simpleTranslation: She does not leave her first permitted status.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends אבוה דשמואל by reading 'leave' in a different way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Leave' does not have to mean leaving a husband. It can mean leaving her permitted status. So even before she marries, the later witnesses do not take away the permission the court already gave her.

keyTerms.meaning: Her first permission, the permitted status she was given

steps.whatToRemember: According to אבוה דשמואל, once the court permits her to marry, later witnesses cannot take that permission away. This is true even if she has not married yet.

phrases.english: She does not leave her first permitted status.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of a word in the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'She does not leave' means she does not leave a husband, so it requires an actual marriage.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'She does not leave' means she does not lose her earlier permission to marry.

steps.title: A captive who says she has witnesses is permitted right away
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a שבויה says she is pure and has witnesses, the court does not wait for them. It permits her right away.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: If she said, 'I was captured, I am pure, and I have witnesses that I am pure,' the court does not say 'Let us wait until the witnesses come.' Instead, it permits her right away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא about a captive woman who claims she stayed pure and says she has witnesses. The court permits her right away, without waiting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Her own word is enough, because 'the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted.' She is the one who told us she was captured, so we also believe her that she is pure. The witnesses she mentions are not needed before the court gives permission.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The Rabbis taught': this opens a ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה that is not in the משנה itself
Pure: here it means she was not violated during captivity

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
If she said: 'I was taken captive, but I am pure,
and I have witnesses that I am pure,'

phrases.aramaic: אֵין אוֹמְרִים: נַמְתִּין עַד שֶׁיָּבֹאוּ עֵדִים,
phrases.english: we do not say: 'We will wait until the witnesses come,'
rather, we permit her right away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא on the same topic that fits אבוה דשמואל's view that court permission counts on its own.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A captive who says she is pure and has witnesses is permitted right away; the court does not wait for the witnesses.

steps.title: Later witnesses who don't know do not cancel her permission
steps.stepSummary: Once she was permitted, witnesses who say 'we don't know' do not make her leave. Witnesses that she was violated do make her leave, even after many children.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they permitted her to marry, and afterward witnesses came and said 'we don't know,' she does not leave. But if witnesses came saying she was violated, she must leave, even if she already has several children.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues. It explains what happens when witnesses show up after the court has already permitted her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses who 'don't know' add nothing, so her permission stays in place. This matches the reading from step 17: once permission is given, it is not taken back. Real testimony that she was violated is different. It shows she was never really allowed, so she must leave even after years of marriage.

keyTerms.meaning: She does not leave (her husband or her permitted status)

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the exact rule שמואל's daughters use in the story that follows: get permission first, and later doubts cannot remove it.

phrases.english: If they permitted her to marry,
and afterward witnesses came,
and said: 'We do not know' —
she does not leave.
But if witnesses came that she was violated,

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ לָהּ כַּמָּה בָּנִים — תֵּצֵא.
phrases.english: even if she has several children, she must leave.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִתִּירוּהָ לִינָּשֵׂא וְאַחַר כָּךְ בָּאוּ עֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with the case of witnesses who come after permission was given.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once permitted, she keeps her status against witnesses who 'don't know'; only witnesses that she was violated make her leave.

steps.title: שמואל questions why his father guarded the captive women
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דשמואל put guards with captive women in נהרדעא. שמואל asks what good that does, since nobody guarded them before.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some captive women came to נהרדעא. שמואל's father placed guards with them. שמואל said to him: 'And until now, who guarded them?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a story. שמואל challenges his father: guarding the women now seems pointless, because the real worry is what already happened during their captivity.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's point is that the women were unguarded the whole time they were captives. Guarding them now does not remove that doubt. His father's answer comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: נהרדעא, a major Jewish city in בבל

phrases.english: There were captive women who came to נהרדעא.
שמואל's father placed guards with them.
שמואל said to him:
And until now, who guarded them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the ברייתא to a story about how captive women were treated.
steps.kashyaTarget: אבוה דשמואל's decision to guard the captive women
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: They were unguarded during captivity, so guarding them now seems to accomplish nothing.

steps.title: His father answers: treat them as you would your own daughters
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דשמואל answers that if they were שמואל's own daughters, he would not treat them so lightly.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: 'If they were your daughters, would you treat them with such disregard?'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל's father answers the challenge. These women deserve to be protected from now on, just like any Jewish woman would be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father does not argue about the past. He says we must not give up on these women because of their captivity, and we should protect their good status from here on. This sets up the next step, where שמואל's own daughters are taken captive.

phrases.english: He said to him:
If they were your daughters,

phrases.aramaic: מִי הֲוֵית מְזַלְזֵל בְּהוּ כּוּלֵּי הַאי?
phrases.english: would you treat them with so much disregard?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers שמואל's challenge from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing: the guards are about protecting the women's dignity and status from now on, not about fixing the past.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Guarding them now is pointless because the doubt comes from their captivity.
steps.terutzMaskana: They deserve protection like any Jewish daughter, so we guard them from now on.

steps.title: שמואל's daughters are taken captive and go to רבי חנינא's study hall
steps.stepSummary: His father's words came true like 'an error from the ruler': שמואל's daughters were captured and brought to ארץ ישראל. They left their captors outside and went into רבי חנינא's study hall.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was 'like an error that comes out from before the ruler.' שמואל's daughters were taken captive and brought up to ארץ ישראל. They left their captors standing outside and went into the study hall of רבי חנינא.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. His father's words, 'if they were your daughters,' came true, and שמואל's own daughters became captives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His father's words are compared to a ruler's mistaken order: once spoken, they come true. The daughters cleverly entered the court before their captors did, so the court would hear their claim before seeing who had captured them.

keyTerms.meaning: Study hall (where the court also sat)

phrases.english: It was 'like an error that comes out from before the ruler,'
phrases.notes: קהלת 10:5. His father's words came true, the way a ruler's mistaken order still gets carried out.

phrases.english: and the daughters of Mar שמואל were taken captive,
and they brought them up to ארץ ישראל.
They left their captors standing outside,
and they went into the study hall of רבי חנינא.
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, 'they,' is part of the corrected wording. It makes clear it was the daughters who went in.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how his father's words in step 21 came true.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: שמואל's daughters were captured and came before רבי חנינא's court without their captors.

steps.title: Each daughter says 'I was captured and I am pure' and is permitted
steps.stepSummary: Each daughter makes the claim from the ברייתא, and the court permits them.
steps.simpleTranslation: This one said, 'I was captured and I am pure,' and that one said, 'I was captured and I am pure.' The court permitted them.
steps.whatsHappening: The daughters use the rule from step 18. Each says she was captured but stayed pure, and the court permits them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No witnesses were present, so their own word, 'the mouth that forbade,' was enough. Because the captors were still outside, nothing yet showed the court otherwise. So they were permitted.

phrases.english: This one said: 'I was taken captive, and I am pure,'
and that one said: 'I was taken captive, and I am pure' —
and they permitted them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: the daughters make their claim in court.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Based on their own claim, the court permitted them to marry, even into כהונה.

steps.title: The captors arrive, but the permission stands; רבי חנינא praises the daughters
steps.stepSummary: The captors came in later, but the daughters were already permitted. רבי חנינא said they must be daughters of great teachers, and it turned out they were שמואל's daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, their captors came in. רבי חנינא said: 'They are daughters of great teachers.' Then it came out that they were the daughters of מר שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends. The captors' arrival does not cancel the permission, and רבי חנינא sees that the daughters knew the הלכה well.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the rule from step 19 in action. Once she is permitted, later doubts do not remove the permission. The daughters knew to speak before their captors appeared, so רבי חנינא guessed they came from a family of great teachers, and he was right.
steps.whatToRemember: A שבויה who says 'I am pure' is permitted right away. Once she is permitted, later doubts (witnesses who don't know, or the captors arriving) do not take it away. Only clear witnesses that she was violated do. שמואל's daughters used exactly this rule.
steps.confusionAlert: The captors coming in does not prove the daughters were violated. It only proves they were captives, which the daughters admitted themselves. So their permission stays.

phrases.english: In the end, their captors came in.
רבי חנינא said:
They are daughters of great teachers.
The matter came to light
that they were the daughters of Mar שמואל.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story and shows the ברייתא's rule from step 19 in action.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Permission given on her own claim stays in force even when the captors appear later. The daughters' wise use of this rule showed they were שמואל's daughters.

steps.title: רבי חנינא tells רב שמן to marry one of the daughters
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא tells רב שמן בר אבא to go take care of his relatives, שמואל's daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנינא said to רב שמן בר אבא: Go and take care of your relatives.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues. Now that the court has permitted שמואל's daughters, רבי חנינא tells a relative of theirs, רב שמן בר אבא, to go take care of them and marry one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the practical result of the court's permission in the last step. רבי חנינא treats the daughters as fully permitted, even to a כהן. That sets up the objection that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Take care of, tend to (here meaning to marry)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חֲנִינָא לְרַב שֶׁמֶן בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chanina said to Rav Shemen bar Abba:
Go out and tend to your relatives.
phrases.notes: He means שמואל's daughters from the story: go take care of them, which here means marry one of them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חֲנִינָא לְרַב שֶׁמֶן בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story by applying the court's permission in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The daughters are fully permitted, so a כהן relative may marry one.

steps.title: רב שמן objects that there are witnesses overseas
steps.stepSummary: רב שמן points out that there are witnesses far away who know the women were captured.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to רבי חנינא: But there are witnesses overseas!
steps.whatsHappening: רב שמן pushes back. The women were permitted on their own word, but there are witnesses far away who know what happened to them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The daughters were believed because of their own claim, with no witnesses to the captivity in court. רב שמן asks whether witnesses who exist somewhere else should change that.

keyTerms.meaning: A country overseas, a far-off place

phrases.english: He said to Rabbi Chanina:
But there are witnesses in a country overseas!
phrases.notes: He means witnesses who know what happened to the women in captivity. רב אשי explains in Step 30 that these were witnesses who saw them violated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חנינא's instruction to marry the daughters.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's ruling that the daughters are permitted.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The permission depended on there being no witnesses, but witnesses to the captivity do exist far away.

steps.title: Far-away witnesses who are not here do not count
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא answers that the witnesses are not here, and witnesses far away cannot forbid her.
steps.simpleTranslation: Right now, anyway, they are not in front of us. Witnesses far up north, and she should be forbidden because of them?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא answers that witnesses who are not in court do not matter. He uses a saying: should a woman be forbidden because of witnesses somewhere far away?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The law goes by what is in front of the court. Witnesses who exist only in theory, in some distant place, have no effect on the woman's status.

phrases.english: Now, in any event, they are not before us.
Witnesses on the north side, and she should be forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב שמן's objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limits the objection: only witnesses who actually come to court count.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The very existence of witnesses anywhere should forbid the women.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses who are not present have no effect, so the women stay permitted.

steps.title: Inference: if witnesses came, the daughters would be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads from רבי חנינא's answer that witnesses who actually came would forbid the daughters.
steps.simpleTranslation: So the reason is that the witnesses did not come. But if witnesses did come, she would be forbidden?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws a conclusion from רבי חנינא's words. This sets up the next move, a challenge to that conclusion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא said the witnesses don't count because they are not here. That suggests that if they did show up, even after the court permitted the women, the women would become forbidden.

phrases.english: The reason is that the witnesses did not come,
but if witnesses came, she would be forbidden?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from רבי חנינא's answer, to prepare a challenge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By implication, witnesses who come to court after the permission would forbid the women.

steps.title: Challenge from שמואל's father: once permitted, she stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: אבוה דשמואל ruled that once the court permits a woman to marry, she stays permitted even before she marries.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't אבוה דשמואל say: Once they permitted her to marry, even though she has not married yet, she stays permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the inference from the last step. It quotes אבוה דשמואל, who said that once a woman is permitted, witnesses who come later do not change that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under אבוה דשמואל's rule, the court's permission already protected שמואל's daughters. So why would רבי חנינא suggest that witnesses arriving later could forbid them?

keyTerms.meaning: That they permitted her to marry

phrases.english: But didn't Shmuel's father say:
Once they permitted her to marry,
even though she has not married!
phrases.notes: The end of the sentence is left unsaid: she stays permitted even if witnesses come later.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference drawn in step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that witnesses who came would forbid the daughters.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: אבוה דשמואל held that the court's permission alone protects her, so later witnesses should not forbid her.

steps.title: רב אשי: the talk was about witnesses who saw actual violation
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the case was about witnesses to the women's defilement, not just to the captivity.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It was said about witnesses to defilement.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי settles the contradiction. רבי חנינא was talking about witnesses who saw the women actually violated.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אבוה דשמואל's rule protects a permitted woman from witnesses who only saw that she was captured. Witnesses who saw that she was actually violated are much stronger, and they would forbid her even after the permission. So the two statements do not conflict.

keyTerms.meaning: Witnesses who saw that she was defiled (actually violated)

steps.whatToRemember: Once a captive woman is permitted to marry, witnesses who only saw the captivity cannot forbid her (אבוה דשמואל). But עדי טומאה, witnesses who saw she was actually violated, would still forbid her (רב אשי).
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of witnesses. עדי שבייה only saw that she was captured. עדי טומאה saw that she was actually violated. Only the second kind can undo the permission.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
It was stated about witnesses of defilement.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי עֵדֵי טוּמְאָה אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from אבוה דשמואל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: the witnesses in question are עדי טומאה, not עדי שבייה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי חנינא meant witnesses to the captivity, which would conflict with אבוה דשמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses to the captivity cannot undo the permission. Only witnesses to actual violation can, so both statements stand.
steps.whyThisMatters: It draws the line between the two kinds of witnesses, which decides when a court's permission for a captive woman can still be undone.
